newsitem.title: INDIA: India expatriate deposit growth slowed by CRR - RBI.
newsitem.headline: India expatriate deposit growth slowed by CRR - RBI.

text.p: The growth of India's foreign currency deposits has slowed after the central bank imposed cash reserve ratio (CRR) requirements to stem capital inflows, a central bank official said on Friday.

"After the imposition of CRR on incremental non-resident Indian deposits, there has been some deceleration in the growth of foreign currency deposits during the current financial year," Deputy Governor Y.V. Reddy of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said.
India's current financial year runs from March 1997 to April 1998.
Reddy was addressing a meeting of the Forex Association of India in the tourist resort of Goa.
Foreign currency swaps were another was of sterilising capital inflows, with the foreign currency purchased by banks being used to finance domestic activites or for investment abroad, Reddy said.
But a thin Indian forex market made them unfeasible.

"Our experience shows that the market is fairly thin and in such a market the use of foreign currency swaps for sterilisation only adds volatility to the forward market unless there is a constant swap window," Reddy added.
Central bank could use outright forward exchange transactions, that is buying outright forward instead of spot, Reddy said.

But this would have the desired effect on the spot rate only if it were not countered by very large spot inflows from participants like FIIs and forward supplies by exporters wishing to take advantage of the increase in premium.
Taxes on capital inflows was another form of dissuading flows that had been considered at one time but deferred because of its attendant disadvantages, Reddy said.
